# Preface

Until now, we have owed most inventions largely to chance; however, through this <term>calculus</term><note>original: "Kalkul." A formal method of systematic calculation or symbolic reasoning.</note>, a law of invention is established. This law shows us, through the study of what is possible, how reality must necessarily exist.

The further advantages that the practitioner gains through this science consist in the fact that, through the constant repetition of the same signs, combinations, and rules, the system imprints itself so deeply into the memory that it becomes indelible.

The operations become increasingly easier; and while other scientific exercises tire the senses and wear down the organs, through this analytical method of our numerical calculus, the spirit is ever more perfected and sharpened the longer it remains active. The signs gradually transition entirely into the <term>imagination</term><note>original: "Einbildungskraft." The mental faculty of forming representations and images.</note>, and through this, human reason can achieve its greatest perfection; for the imagination becomes—in everything one forms from it—orderly, methodical, and analogous to the <term>understanding</term><note>original: "Verstand." The faculty of the mind that processes concepts and judgments.</note>.

# Preface

"Images," says <term>Lambert</term><note>Johann Heinrich Lambert (1728–1777) was a Swiss polymath who made significant contributions to logic and mathematics. He was a contemporary of Kant and sought to develop a symbolic language for thought.</note>, "which possess nothing other than certain fixed ratios—which have already been combined a thousandfold and always according to the same rules—must themselves continue these combinations within the <term>imagination</term><note>original: "Imagination." Referring to the mental faculty of visualizing and manipulating concepts.</note> into infinity, and the human spirit can derive the greatest skill from them."

Critics and those clinging to old prejudices may speak against it, object, doubt, and find fault as they please; we are not concerned here with mere opinion. One never disputes over the truth, but only over opinions.

The abundance of practical examples appearing in this section provides everyone with the proof they need; personal conviction is the most decisive refutation of any doubt.

Far be it from me to present this science of the <term>calculus of nature</term><note>original: "Kalkul der Natur." A system of symbolic logic or calculation that the author believes reflects the inherent laws of the physical and spiritual world.</note> as a new invention; rather, I consider it the oldest science—one that humanity perhaps once possessed in its complete purity and has since lost:—

# Preface

...easily, but also not entirely lost; rather, it is lost only for the great and common crowd, which always clings to multiplicity and is incapable of thinking its way into what is simple.

It remains forever true what <term>Lambert</term><note>Johann Heinrich Lambert (1728–1777) was a Swiss polymath. In the 18th century, he was famous for trying to apply mathematical precision to philosophy and logic.</note> said with so much truth: “The <term>Analyst</term><note>In this context, an 'Analyst' is someone who uses the methods of mathematics and symbolic logic to break down complex ideas into certain truths.</note> proceeds from truth to truth; everything is luminous around him; whichever dark spot he may act upon, there he sees light arise. — What encouragement, what pleasure, what intellectual delight, what rapture must bless the spirit that raises itself with the greatest ease into a region where nothing exists but order, symmetry, and perfection! — The <term>Philosopher</term><note>The author uses 'Philosopher' here in a slightly critical sense, referring to those who rely on abstract speculation and vague descriptions ('qualities') rather than precise logical systems.</note>, on the other hand, gropes about in the dark by a barely dawning light among phantoms of qualities, which, raised from the chaos with great effort, lose themselves again in indeterminacy. If he has succeeded in reaching a few ideas, in chaining a few conclusions together, these are but drops in a sea, which flow back into it again without firm boundaries. With an indescribably laborious effort, he thus finds little more than — probabilities.”

# Preface

Indeed, it is not easy for disorderly minds to think according to order, for order exists only for those who are themselves orderly. Many will judge this <term>numerical calculus</term><note>original: "Zahlenkalkul." This refers to the author's method of using mathematical-style logic or symbolic calculation to reach philosophical certainties, much like the "Analyst" mentioned on the previous page.</note> just as the village schoolmaster once judged the writings of <term>Pope</term><note>Alexander Pope (1688–1744) was a famous English poet. His work "An Essay on Man" was a major philosophical poem of the era, though its density and wit often drew criticism from less sophisticated readers.</note>. "The fellow is a fool," he said, "for I do not understand him." Few people are so modest that, when they do not understand something, they are willing to be convinced that the fault lies within themselves; instead, they shift the blame for their ignorance onto the subject matter with total confidence.

However, this book is not written for such people. Where there is light, one must possess an organ for seeing. It is enough for me if the modest seeker finds a closer path to the truth.

# Monadology,<note>A "Monad" (from the Greek *monas*, meaning unity or alone) refers to a fundamental, indivisible, and indestructible unit of reality. In the philosophical tradition of the 17th and 18th centuries—most notably associated with Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz—monads are the "simple substances" that make up the entire universe, each reflecting the whole from its own perspective.</note>

->or<-

## Doctrine of the Law of Unity.

---

<vocab>Monadology, Doctrine, Law, Unity</vocab>

<summary>This is the title page for a treatise on Monadology, which the author defines as the study or science of the "Law of Unity."</summary>

<keywords>Monadology, Law of Unity, Metaphysics, Simple Substances, Philosophy of Unity</keywords>

<image-desc>An etched landscape illustration within a rectangular border at the top of the page. On the left side are ruins of two stone towers and some low-roofed houses nestled among trees. In the foreground, a figure is depicted near a body of water. In the background, a distant city skyline with walls and spires is visible across a flat landscape under a streaked sky.</image-desc>

### I.
## What Thinking Is in Humans.

In humans there resides a <term>faculty<note>German: *Vermögen*; in 18th-century philosophy, this refers to an inherent power or capacity of the mind, such as reason or imagination.</note></term> to behold objects and to take in the images of these objects.

The power which is the primary cause of this faculty we call the **power of thought**; and the consciousness of these received images, we call **ideas** or **concepts**.

Because man is therefore a being who possesses the capacity for thinking, there must exist in nature a law, a relationship, according to which his thinking conducts itself; for everything in nature follows unchanging laws.

The true law of every thing is only that which accords with the order of nature, for only the eternal order and the eternal relationships of things provide us with the basis upon which we must seek the order and the relationships or laws of things.

<vocab>Thinking, Power of Thought, Consciousness, Ideas, Concepts, Law, Nature, Order</vocab>

<meta>signature: A</meta>
<meta>catchword: The</meta>

<summary>This opening page defines human thought as a natural faculty that captures images of objects, forming concepts and ideas. It argues that human cognition is not random but is governed by the same immutable laws and eternal order that rule the rest of the natural world.</summary>
<keywords>cognition, faculty of thought, natural law, consciousness, ideas, concepts, philosophy of nature, Enlightenment epistemology</keywords>

--- Page 36 ---
<meta>This page continues the investigation into the relationship between human thought and natural law, moving from the definition of thought to the methodology of "correct" thinking.</meta>

The law of thinking can be none other than the law of nature’s own production; for to think means to take in images of things outside of ourselves, and things in nature are arranged in an orderly sequence one after another.

If we therefore take them in according to this order by which nature assembles things, only then can we think correctly.

### 2.
## What thinking correctly means.

Nature works within according to unchanging laws; everything external is a <term>realization<note>German: *Realisation*; the physical manifestation or "making real" of an internal law or idea.</note></term> of what is internal. Nothing can exist in the <term>appearance<note>German: *Erscheinung*; a philosophical term referring to the world as it presents itself to our senses, as opposed to how it might exist independently of us.</note></term> of a thing that does not first have its basis in what lies beneath that appearance.

If I now observe existing things in this <term>corporeal world<note>German: *Körperwelt*; the material world composed of physical bodies.</note></term> according to the very same principles by which nature constructs, forms, and assembles them, then I am thinking correctly; for I am no longer thinking of characteristics abstracted from things, but of the thing itself.

### 3.
## What it means to think *after the fact* and *from the beginning*.

A human being can think <term>after the fact<note>Latin: *a posteriori*; reasoning based on observed facts and experiences already encountered.</note></term> and <term>from the beginning<note>Latin: *a priori*; reasoning from self-evident principles or causes that precede experience.</note></term>; that is to say: he can think organically and <term>genetically<note>German: *genetisch*; here meaning to understand something by its "genesis" or the process by which it was produced, rather than just its final form.</note></term>, according to the principles that underlie appearances, or according to the appearances themselves.

<vocab>Law of thinking, production of nature, realization, corporeal world, principles, a posteriori, a priori, organic thinking, genetic thinking</vocab>

<summary>This page argues that correct thinking must mirror the productive order of nature, moving beyond mere observations to understand the underlying principles of objects. It distinguishes between thinking based on experience (a posteriori) and thinking based on the internal origins or "genesis" of objects (a priori).</summary>
<keywords>epistemology, natural philosophy, a priori, a posteriori, genetic thinking, realization, appearances, laws of nature</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the methodology of thought, specifically distinguishing between the "genetic" and "organic" approaches to understanding nature, before transitioning to the role of the senses.</meta>

To think <term>after the fact<note>Latin: *a posteriori*; knowledge gained through observation and experience rather than theoretical deduction.</note></term> means that one ascends from appearances toward the principles of things:

To think <term>from the beginning<note>Latin: *a priori*; knowledge that proceeds from theoretical deduction or self-evident principles rather than observation.</note></term> means that one thinks of these principles as the very constructions of those appearances.

Nature expresses its effects starting from the power of a **unity** and passing into **multiplicity**;—and then moves from multiplicity back again to unity; from the simple to the composite; from the composite back to the simple.

If I consider things from the first viewpoint, then I am considering them <term>genetically<note>German: *genetisch*; an approach that seeks to understand a thing by looking at its origin or how it was "generated" from a seed or principle.</note></term>, or in their principles:

The first is called thinking *from the beginning*—viewing things within their unity:

The second is thinking *after the fact*—viewing things within their multiplicity—within the composite.

### 6.
### How Errors in Thinking Arise from a Lack of Knowledge regarding the Construction of Ideas.

The soul is not content with the mere intuition and contemplation of its mental images; it is of a far more active and busy nature; it assembles and compares.

Since it now forms new compositions from existing compositions, yet does not know the laws by which Nature composes, it must here again make false judgments and conclusions, because it does not perceive that which constructs its ideas.

Can a person calculate correctly if they do not know the internal nature of numbers, or do not know the level of progression <note>German: *Progressions-Stufe*; refers to the mathematical order or place value in a sequence.</note> on which their number stands? Do not all errors or mistakes in arithmetic arise from a sensory oversight, when I take one number for another than it truly is, or fail to follow the order of progression?

## Without Knowledge of the Construction of Ideas, One Cannot Think Correctly.

Without knowledge of the construction of ideas, we can therefore never think correctly. Mathematics, as the only science of convincing truths, receives its clarity <note>original: *Evidenz*; in this context, it refers to self-evident certainty or the quality of being indubitable.</note> precisely because its conclusions are grounded in pure, intuitive concepts, whereby it becomes a science of vivid perception <note>original: *Anschaulichkeit*; the quality of being able to be visualized or directly grasped by the mind's eye.</note>.

The teachers of logic <note>original: *Vernunftlehrer*; literally "teachers of reason," referring to the philosophers and logicians of the Enlightenment tradition.</note> call "simple ideas" those that are found in the soul in a uniform shape, without variety or composition; yet this "simple" thing always remains a composite in Nature, which can again be dissolved into its principles.

It is indeed characteristic of the understanding to form a unity out of multiplicity and to contemplate this unity; yet all unities that the understanding receives through mental images and sensory intuition <note>original: *sinnliche Anschauung*; the direct perception of an object via the senses.</note> are not true unities; they are merely relative unities. For example, a number such as 3 or 6, when considered on its own, can be a unity in respect to my intuition, but by no means in Nature, in which it behaves according to the progression <note>Referencing the mathematical order or place-value system mentioned on the previous page.</note> that constitutes its essence.

One can, therefore, never mix the unities of appearances <note>original: *Erscheinungen*; things as they are perceived by the senses, rather than things as they are in themselves.</note> with the [true] unities, nor with the first principles.

## 8.

### The Laws of Thought Lie Architectonically <note>Refers to "architectonic" in the Kantian sense: the art of building a systematic structure of knowledge based on internal principles of reason.</note> in Reason, and are Realized in Nature.

### 8.

### The Laws of Thought are Architecturally Situated in Reason, and Realized in Nature.

Since we think through mental images <note>original: *Ideenbilder*; literally "idea-pictures," referring to the mental representations or concepts we use to grasp reality.</note>, there must necessarily be laws in place according to which we think correctly; for if everything in nature stands according to immutable laws in a harmonic order, then there must also be relationships by which thinking beings can perceive this harmonic order exactly as it exists in nature.

Experience shows us that we ascend based on experience <note>original: *a posteriori*; reasoning from observed facts back to their causes.</note> from the composite to the simple. ### 9.

## **Unity is the simplest idea—the principle of ideas—without it, one cannot think correctly.**

The most common and simplest idea we have is the idea of unity, or of one.

By constantly repeating this unity within itself and keeping the various combinations in mind, we arrive at all the infinite compositions of numbers, wherein we immediately perceive an infinite diversity; nevertheless, these ideas are clearly distinct from one another, in that the addition of a single unity constitutes a number that is just as precisely distinguished from the one immediately preceding it as any two of the most distant ideas are distinguished from one another. <note>The author is arguing that the difference between 1 and 2 is just as "distinct" and logically absolute as the difference between 1 and 1,000,000.</note>

However, so that the understanding <note>original: *Verstand*; the faculty of the mind responsible for logic and conceptual processing.</note> does not lose itself in the contemplation of those infinite combinations of which unity is capable, it proceeds in an orderly fashion, step by step; and by beginning with the original idea itself, it then follows it through all its transformations, as they are produced by the constantly repeated addition of one unity to another.

Thus, arithmetic numbers arise by always allowing one to follow another in an orderly series, and by designating the various combinations that gradually emerge with specific names.

### 11.

### **We attain the representation of intermediate things in nature through numbers. The same law also leads us to the discovery of intermediate ideas in thinking.**

We owe our most precise and distinct concepts of intermediate things <note>original: *Mitteldinge*; objects or entities that occupy a middle ground or transitional state between two points.</note> in nature to numbers. It is specifically through the intuition <note>original: *Intuition*; in this philosophical context, it refers to the direct mental "seeing" or immediate perception of an object.</note> of numerical progression that we recognize, in a single act of perception, not only the step a number occupies within the orderly sequence, but also its relationship to other numbers. These serve as the intermediate numbers that bridge the gap from one specific number to another. Furthermore, we generally observe that all our ideas of magnitudes <note>original: *Größen*; any measurable extent, such as size, weight, or volume.</note>—especially when they begin to become quite extensive—only achieve clarity within us through the representation of the middle parts, which are situated, so to speak, between the two ends.

### 12.

### **Human judgment and inner feeling operate according to intermediate ideas.**

When we see an object at a considerable distance from us, we will be able to determine its distance provided that we can clearly see the objects—such as houses, etc.—that lie in between.

### 14.
### By which law the human spirit measures duration.

For this very reason, we can understand why the duration of a day can seem long to one person and, for another, the same duration of an identical physical phenomenon of time can seem short. This depends entirely on the **intermediate circumstances** <note>original: *Mittelumstände*</note> by which the spirit <term>Spirit (Geist): In this period, *Geist* refers to the mental faculty, intellect, or the seat of consciousness.</term> measures; the less the spirit pays attention to what lies as a medium between the object and the subject, the shorter the duration seems to it; however, the more it directs its attention to the intermediate things, the longer the measure of its time becomes.

A poet, or a man of business whose soul applies its entire attention to the completion of a task, pays no heed to the intermediate circumstances, and time will always seem too short for him.

### 16.

## On the numerical law in thinking.

Through numerical concepts, the intellect is not only able to measure duration, extension, and motion, etc., but also to form a division of complex concepts into certain classes, whereby it gains a great facilitation of its intuitiveness <term>Intuitiveness (Anschaulichkeit): The ability to form a clear mental image or grasp a concept directly.</term>.

1. knows the construction of his concepts—the parts, if I may express myself so, of which his idea consists; and then

### 21.

## What ideas are in nature, and that the laws of nature lie beneath the fundamental laws of the understanding

An **idea** is that which, outside of the human understanding, lies at the foundation of a thing through the operation of the first principle <term>First Principle (erstes Princip): The primary source or fundamental cause from which all other things flow.</term>; it is the reason why a thing appears and can be grasped as a distinct object.

Ideas are the constructions of these principles, which become intuitive to us through an active, working unity.

Kant <note>Immanuel Kant (1724–1804), the central figure in modern philosophy who argued that the mind organizes our experiences.</note> says very beautifully that, without exception, all laws of nature lie under higher principles of the **understanding**, for the understanding is the faculty of **concepts**. Consequently, the ideas that constitute these concepts must lie outside our understanding, because they construct—as pure principles—that which our understanding perceives within those concepts. Even in the realm of ideas, our understanding follows a numerical progression <note>This likely refers to the "categories" of the understanding, which Kant organized into groups of three (quantity, quality, relation, modality).</note>.

Ideas — Concepts — Feeling — Sensation.

What we perceive through the **senses**, we feel internally through the **spirit**; what we feel through the spirit, we grasp through the **understanding**; and what we grasp through the understanding, we contemplate through **reason** <term>Reason (Vernunft): Here used as the highest capacity of the mind, which looks beyond physical objects to the underlying "principles" of reality.</term> within the principles themselves.

Therefore, Ideas, Concepts, Feeling, and Sensation must never be confused with one another.

### 23.

## On Representations, Perceptions, Intuitions, Concepts, Notions, and Ideas.

There are representations, perceptions, sensations, intuitions <note>original: "Intuitus"</note>, concepts <note>original: "Conceptus"</note>, notions, and ideas.

A mental image or thought in general is a **representation** <note>original: "Repräsentation" or "Vorstellung"</note>.

If this representation is accompanied by consciousness, it is a **perception** <note>original: "Perceptio"</note>.

A perception that refers merely to the subject as a modification of its own state is **sensation**—*Sensatio* <note>original: "Sensatio"; the internal feeling triggered by a stimulus, rather than the identification of the object itself.</note>.

### 25.
## On the Laws of Construction in Nature.

It is certain that, in order to have a clear intuitive concept of a thing, I must know the construction of that thing—the components that make the thing what it is.

This construction, or the principles of things, must possess certain necessary relationships according to which they construct the thing; knowledge of these relationships allows us to perceive the construction of ideas. For example: if I say "3" or "4," I only know how to distinguish 3 from 4 by the difference in their form <note>The author likely refers to the written numerals themselves.</note>, but I do not yet have an intuitive concept of either 3 or 4. However, if I know the principles of 3 and 4, or that which constitutes 3 and 4, then I have a clear perception, and indeed one that is *a priori* <note>original: "a priori"; referring to knowledge that exists in the mind independently of sensory experience, such as the basic rules of logic or math.</note>. For example: . . . = 3; . . . . = 4. From this intuition of the principles of numbers, pure arithmetical truths arise.

The great question, therefore, remains: can we know the construction of ideas in all objects, and how is all of this to be approached?

We observe in all things of appearance <note>original: "Erscheinungen"; the world as we perceive it through our senses, as opposed to the "thing-in-itself."</note> that in everything that is, everything that exists:

### 27.
## Concepts concerning Unity in Nature and Principle.

When we represent several objects within a single concept, we call what we are imagining a "unity." For example, within an <term>individual (originally *individuo*; a single, distinct entity)</term>, we conceive of all the parts that construct this individual under one single concept.

All examples by which we imagine unities can clearly convince us that unity exists only in our conception, and by no means in the individual itself, which is not a true unity but rather something composed of many parts.

The question then arises: is there no true unity? Experience and nature teach us that in time and space—where <term>extension (the property of occupying space)</term> and magnitudes exist—there can be no real unity, because every extension is subject to measurement, and every magnitude is subject to being made smaller or larger. <note>In philosophy, a "true unity" must be indivisible; since anything in the physical world can be divided or measured, it cannot be a true unity.</note>

That which lies at the foundation of all extension and magnitude, and which exists outside of space and time as a <term>principle (originally *princip*; a fundamental source or primary element)</term>—that alone can be a true unity:

For that which is perfectly One is not different; it is One.

We thus obtain, through the observation of the above laws, a certain measure for the forces, effects, consequences, and realizations; and since everything in the universe <note>original: *Universo*</note> consists of forces, effects, consequences, and realizations, we are able to eavesdrop on the most secret <term>mechanisms (German: *Schrauben*; literally "screws")</term> of the universe. We learn to think, work, act, and realize according to unchangeable laws, as one law always teaches us another, and we are enabled to bring about the greatest things in nature.

The laws for thinking give us the laws for working; the laws for working the laws for acting; the laws for acting the laws for realizing.

From all of this we see that the first Principle is a thinking Principle.

The first Principle is the source of the purest reason.

### 29.
# On Forces and Primordial Force.

Whatever is capable of increase or decrease is generally called a <term>magnitude (German: *Größe*; a mathematical term for any measurable quantity)</term>.

Under the concept of magnitude, everything that is capable of increase or decrease can therefore be understood ——

->Number, extension, line, surface, body.<-

That which is incapable of increase and decrease cannot be called magnitude, but rather <term>force (German: *Kraft*)</term>, the cause of magnitude, or a Principle.

The Principle of magnitude underlies magnitudes as their cause, without itself possessing the properties of magnitudes, and relates [to them] as force relates to effect.

### 31.
## On the Realm of Appearance and its Law.

In appearance <term>Erscheinung; the physical, observable world</term>, nothing can manifest that does not underlie the appearance as a principle.

The principles are therefore the laws of the appearances, and lie outside of the appearances. They are only conceivable, but they become mathematically certain to us because we can view their laws in their realization as a consequence, just as we think of the principles in the intellect as forces according to the laws of numbers.

In the writings of antiquity, one finds an extremely interesting symbol regarding the human faculty of cognition.

Cognition, they said, occurs:

1. through the senses
2. through the reason <term>Vernunft; often distinguished from the "intellect" (Verstand) as a higher capacity for grasping universal truths</term>

### 32.

## On the Revelation of the First Principle through Nature, Writing, and Language.

Writing and language are therefore the only modes of instruction for the human spirit.

The First Principle also has its language and its writing, through which we receive instruction regarding its revelation.

The writing lies in the realization of nature—its language in the forces; the former follows the Law of Four <term>Viergesetz; previously defined as the law governing material manifestation and physical form</term>, the latter follows the Law of Three <term>Dreygesetz; the law governing spiritual activity and movement</term> of unity.

Man learns to read within nature when he knows the letters of nature.

These letters are the principles of things, and they relate to the 4 modes of perception <term>Anschauungsarten; the specific ways the mind views or intuitis reality</term>.

In this lies the great mystery of the alphabet of nature with 4 letters, about which one finds so much in the mysteries <note>This likely refers to the Tetragrammaton, the four-letter name of God, or the ancient concept of the four elements as the "alphabet" of the physical world</note>.

These 4 modes of perception are the 4 wheels of the Quadriga <term>Quadriga; a chariot drawn by four horses, often used in ancient philosophy to symbolize the soul or the movement of the divine through the universe</term>, upon which Unity travels through the worlds.

The voice of the Deity lies in the Law of Three of nature. If I know this Law of Three, then I know the progression of divine ideas that underlie all things in order as principles, and I learn to understand the language that is peculiar to the Deity, which is the realization of its ideas.

### 34.

## The Understanding follows the numerical progression of Nature in the composition of its ideas.

The understanding <term>Verstand; the faculty of the mind responsible for processing sensory data and forming logical concepts</term> assembles its ideas and proceeds numerically through various classes of concepts.

Just as the progression from the first number occurs through middle numbers to the highest number, so too is the progression of the understanding from the simple concept to the composite through various intermediate stages <term>Mittel-Stuffen; the transitional steps between a basic idea and a complex system</term>.

This is also the true manner and way in which we must proceed with explanations in order to bring our concepts into the understanding of others:

for since the series begins with simple and easy connections, and proceeds through various stages in successive order, where one always rises above the other in respect to the degree of order, it is clear that in a series of explanations which express these ideas, this progression of stages <term>Stuffengang; a graduated or step-by-step sequence</term> must be observed.

Just as the understanding goes to work in thinking, so nature proceeds in her compositions. The understanding can only follow her laws if it wishes to think correctly.

## 38.

### 40.
## The laws of creation are progressive laws.

The laws of creation—the laws according to which the **first force** expressed itself outside of itself—are progressive laws.

Time lies at the foundation of space.

The laws that constitute space lie within time.

The laws that constitute time lie within **Unity**.

From this, three possible <term>progressions</term> <note>sequences or series where each term is derived from the previous one according to a specific rule</note> follow:
the **thinkable**—in the force.
The **progressive**—in time.
The **geometric**—in space.

Therein lie the highest truths of mathematics, which until now knew only two progressions, namely the arithmetical and the geometrical—the countable and the measurable. The first, or **thinkable** progression, was missing:

For before I count, I must be able to think; then I count; and only when I count can I measure.

Thus, there are three progressions in mathematics and not two; and all three behave according to the same laws, only at different <term>stages</term> <note>original: *Stuffen* (modern *Stufen*); refers to levels or degrees of manifestation</note>.

Beyond space and time, the law of Unity reigns.

In time, the law of progression.

### 44.
## Unity is no number.

Unity cannot be a number, for a number is something composite <note>something made of multiple parts or units added together</note>; unity is therefore the source of numbers without ever being a number itself.

### 45.
## In unity, all is one.

In unity, everything is one, for unity is the law of unity—1 times 1 is 1.

In unity, all actions are simultaneous.

Force, effect, and consequence are one.

Force, will, and deed are one.

There is nothing in a number in its realization that is not in <term>potentiality</term> <note>original Latin: *potentia*; refers to a power that exists but has not yet been acted out</note> within the unity.

Unity is force; force increases in the number as it ascends toward unity;—the simpler the number, the more force it possesses.

Therefore, the first principle <note>original: *Princip*; the foundational source or origin of all things</note> of things is threefold according to its essence, and yet it is one.

### 48.

## Outside of time, Unity can only be conceived as Unity.

Outside of progression, Unity can only be conceived as Unity; — its properties as the source of numbers only become conceivable through progression in time.

The property of Unity, in its progression outside of itself, is to produce a similar unity, which however is only a <term>type</term> <note>original: *Typus*; here meaning a model, archetype, or representative form rather than the thing itself</note>, an image of itself.

->1 and 1 is 2.<-

1 and 1 is the beginning of progression, considered in time;

In space and time: action and counter-action;

effect and reaction;

force and phenomenon.

In time — point and progression;

in space — progression and line.

In space and time — surface and body. <note>In this context, "body" (*Körper*) refers to a three-dimensional geometric solid or physical object.</note>

# The first Principle is the source of thinking beings.

To produce images outside of oneself is called to create. <note>In this context, the author uses "images" (*Bilder*) to mean reflections or manifestations of a central idea.</note>

In the universe, there is therefore only one true essence <term>essence</term> <note>original: *Wesenheit*; refers to the fundamental nature or "being-ness" of a thing</note>: the first Principle.

Everything that exists outside of the Principle is an image of this essence:

Just as all numbers are images of Unity that lie outside of Unity.

The capacity to receive images, we call **thinking power** <term>thinking power</term> <note>original: *Denkkraft*; often translated as "intellect" or "faculty of thought"</note>.

The first Principle takes the images outside itself back in, because Unity takes all numbers back in. <note>This suggests a cyclical or emanative process where all things return to their source.</note>

The first Principle is thus the source of all thinking beings.

Outside of itself, the first Principle thinks only impressions of its essence; — within itself, the first Principle thinks only itself.

The order in which the first Principle thinks its impressions outside of itself lies unchangeably within the Principle itself, according to the law of its progression of Unity and 3-fold power <term>3-fold power</term> <note>original: *3 — Kraft*; likely a reference to a triad or trinity within the creative process</note>.

Purest reason, therefore, lies in Unity itself as the basis of progression.

The first Principle is the source of all things.

### 51.

## The first Principle is eternal, equal, and infinite.

The Principle alone—Unity alone—is infinite.

The infinite is therefore not the **composite** <note>original: *Zusammengesetzte*; anything made of multiple parts. The author argues that the truly infinite must be simple and indivisible, rather than a vast collection of parts.</note>, but Unity.

## Matter, or the countable, is not a necessary being; only the Principle or Unity is necessary.

### I.

# Everything that exists must first exist as possible within the law of purest reason.

Everything that exists must first exist as possible within the law of <term>purest reason</term> <note>German: *reinsten Vernunft*. In the context of 18th and 19th-century philosophy, this refers to the fundamental capacity of the mind to understand principles that are independent of sensory experience.</note>.

The laws of purest reason are the laws of <term>unity</term>, which, when considered in themselves, are purest reason itself; outside of themselves, they are the source of all ideas.

Purest reason, viewed as the source of ideas, has the immutable law of progression as the foundation of its ideas, for this law is the <term>law of construction</term> <note>German: *Construktionsgesetz*. This refers to the systematic rules by which complex ideas or structures are built up from simpler principles.</note> of ideas according to the essence of unity.

As purest reason thinks, so it also wills according to that very same law; — and as it wills, so it acts and realizes itself: —

or, to put it another way, purest reason, <term>self-activity</term> <note>German: *Selbstthätigkeit*. This term describes the mind's or nature's inherent power to act and develop from within itself, rather than being moved by external forces.</note>, and the realization of the primary active force in nature all behave according to these same laws of unity.

From this arise four orders of the <term>system of creation</term>, namely:

### 2.
## On the Essential Law of Unity.

When Unity expresses itself outside of itself, this expression occurs through the Law of Three <note>German: *Dreygesetz*. In Western esoteric traditions, the "Law of Three" often represents the creative process where two opposing forces (active and passive) are reconciled by a third to produce a result.</note>, as:

->Force, Effect, Consequence.<-
->Law, Means, Purpose.<-

Every force follows this same law.

Considered outside of time, force includes effect and consequence within itself, as it were, so that force, effect, and consequence form only a single unity; but within time, the expression occurs in a threefold progression, as:

->Force, Effect, Consequence:<-

for no force can express itself without an effect, and no effect can exist without a consequence.

Following the law of the expression of the Triple-Force <note>German: *Dreykraft*.</note> outside of itself, this consequence produces a further progression, which behaves according to the Law of Four <note>German: *Viergesetz*. This refers to the movement from the spiritual triad into the fourfold realm of material reality or "realization."</note>, as:

-><gloss>4</gloss> Realization, <gloss>5</gloss> Relation, <gloss>6</gloss> Order, <gloss>7</gloss> Existence of a thing:<-

and these two laws together determine the great Law of Seven <note>German: *Siebengesetz*. The combination of the Trinity (3) and the Quaternary (4) produces the Septenary (7), a number frequently used in historical philosophy to represent the complete scale of nature or the finished work of creation.</note> of nature, according to which everything that exists conducts itself; for if something exists, there must be

1. a force that expresses itself.
2. The expression must have an effect.
3. This effect, a consequence.
4. This consequence, a realization.
5. The realization, a relation.

<note>The list ends abruptly here at point 5; it is likely continued on the next page to reach the full seven points mentioned in the text.</note>

A group or set of seven; in Western esotericism, the Septenary represents the complete scale of manifestation, from the divine to the material.</note> of the Mysteries.

If I consider the first rational principle <term>Princip: the fundamental source or basis of something; in this context, the divine or original mind</term> outside of time and space, I can only think of it as Unity — as the primal force <term>Urkraft: literally "original force"; the fundamental energy from which all other powers derive</term> of all forces —

as a force that existed before time, and is therefore eternal — —

as a force that is independent of time, and is therefore immutable — —

I discover a motive for this manifestation of force, which in the first thinking principle is called Love <note>original: "Liebe"</note>, or the manifestation of the first primal force to bring forth similar forces outside of itself, and to reunite them with it according to the essence of the quality of this primal force.

That which exists outside of the first principle gives me the concept of Truth <note>original: "Wahrheit"</note>.

### 4.
### On the Will of the First Rational Principle.

The first rational principle <term>Princip: a philosophical term for the ultimate source or fundamental cause of all things, often used here as a rationalist synonym for God</term> is the source of all pure ideas; the impulse for the realization <note>original: "Realisationtrieb"; the inherent drive or pressure for an abstract idea to become a manifest reality</note> of these pure ideas, according to the purest essence of its perfections, is what one calls the Will in the first principle—which is therefore necessarily as pure as the first idea.

In the first rational principle, no ideas other than those of the highest perfection are possible, for Unity is the most perfect of all beings.

It is the source of order; therefore, its essence <term>Wesenheit: the inner nature or "beingness" of a thing that makes it what it is</term> becomes its own law, according to which it realizes all possible purest ideas—which are eternally present to it—following the most perfect order.

The power within the first principle to be able to realize the most perfect ideas of its essence is, when considered as an attribute, called Omnipotence.

The motive to realize these ideas according to its highest perfection is called Love.

Omnipotence is thus the first fundamental force, and the realization of this fundamental force is Love;

the expression is Truth;

the manner of expression is Wisdom;

the purpose is Goodness;

the relationship is Justice;

## The First Principle is the Source of All Order.

The First Principle is the source of all order, for the harmony <note>original: "Uebereinstimmung," implying a perfect correspondence or agreement between parts</note> of omnipotence, love, truth, wisdom, goodness, and justice within this principle constitutes its order.

What is order in God is harmony in the spirit, regularity in actions, and proportion in the physical world. This order manifests itself everywhere, both internally and externally.

Internally, there is power, effect, consequence, thought, will, deed: —

Thus, there is an order for the powers, an order for the effects, an order for the consequences — an order for thinking, an order for willing, an order for acting.

### Basis of the Moral Order.

In the moral order, everything functions according to lawfulness, purposiveness <note>original: "Zweckmäßigkeit." This refers to the quality of being suited to a specific end or goal.</note>, and the final purpose.

If this order is disturbed—if the purpose is turned into the law, or the law is turned into the purpose—then disorder and confusion arise.

Moral goodness rests upon this order; moral evil rests upon this disorder.

The law of virtue is purposiveness, by which virtue must be guided. It serves as the bond between the law and the final purpose.

The human soul possesses three volitional drives — the intellect, *irascibility* <note>original: "Irascibilität," referring to the "spirited" part of the soul associated with courage, anger, and the will to overcome obstacles.</note>, and *concupiscence* <note>original: "Concupiscenz," referring to the "desiring" part of the soul associated with physical needs and sensory pleasures.</note>; or, the faculty of understanding, the faculty of desire, and the faculty of aversion <note>The faculty of "aversion" is the instinct to turn away from or avoid what is perceived as harmful or evil.</note>.

--- Page 156 ---
<meta>This page continues the discussion from the previous page regarding the faculties of the soul, specifically moving from the general definition of the "faculty of aversion" into the distinction between the "outer" and "inner" man and their respective governing laws.</meta>

The outer man perceives through the senses, and his faculty of desire and his faculty of aversion <note>The "faculty of aversion" (original: *Aversionsvermögen*) is the psychological impulse to pull away from things perceived as harmful or unpleasant.</note> behave according to the nature of his sensation and the consciousness of this sensation or feeling.

He judges everything according to sensory perceptions. Therein lies the law of the sensory man. He wants the sensory good that he perceives within the realm of the senses; he shuns the evil or the unpleasant. The measure of his perceptions is sensuality. — This is what one calls the **animal-man**, for he acts according to his sensory drives and lusts. <note>The term "animal-man" (*Thiermensch*) describes a person who lives solely on the level of physical instinct and biological necessity, lacking spiritual or moral direction.</note>

The inner man does not have perception excited by sensuality as his measure, but rather knowledge through the intellect as the measure of his feelings and actions. According to the measure of this feeling, the soul-drive relates to the moral good, and the faculty of aversion relates to moral evil — — a law striving in a direction entirely opposed to sensuality.

Through the spiritual law <note>original: *Geistgesetz*. This refers to the rational or divine principles that govern the higher functions of the human soul.</note> alone is man capable of recognizing the order, and the outer man should submit himself according to this recognition. From this we see that the spiritual law existed before the law of sensuality, because the spiritual law has order as its foundation. Order existed before disorder in nature, and truth before error; for disorder arose through the deviation from order, and error through the misunderstanding of truth.

### 7. Nature and Revelation.

Nature is called the expression of power <note>Original: *Kraftäußerung*. This term describes the outward manifestation or "uttering" of an internal force.</note> of a primal force <note>Original: *Urkraft*.</note>. It can therefore never be conflated with that force, and it stands in an entirely different relationship to it.

Physical nature can therefore be called the organ <note>The author uses "organ" here in the classical sense: a tool or instrument through which a higher power acts.</note> of God’s expression of power.

God and nature relate to one another as the soul relates to the body; for without God, nature ceases to exist.

The expression of power is the manifestation of the revelation of force.

The first forms of letters were anything but arbitrary; they were hieroglyphic signs of the manifestation of inner forces. The ancients formed their first letters according to the way these forces were revealed through the speech organs.

Based on observations of how the inner spirit expresses itself in various forms through the throat, tongue, teeth, lips, and mouth, the ancients shaped their letters.

The Hebrew letters are the most remarkable. I shall explain only a few principles of the whole system.

A is a free tone without form. They attributed this vowel to the first power.

E is a narrower tone, during which the throat constricts slightly. They attributed this to the expression of power <note>original: "Kraft-Aeußerung"</note> that set limits upon its own infinity. <note>In this mystical system, E represents the point where the infinite starts to take on a specific shape or "limit."</note>

To prevent vice, desires and passions must be subjected to the laws of order.

Errors depend on our way of thinking; cravings <note>original: "Gelüste"; refers to impulsive or carnal appetites</note> depend on our will.

Reason <term>Verstand</term> and will must therefore be cultivated, and this occurs when people are taught what law, means, and purpose <note>original: "Zweck"; often translated as "end" in philosophical contexts, referring to the ultimate goal of an action</note> are in nature, for only the confusion of this progression produces all evil.

Self-love and interest must never be the purpose, but rather the means, under the legislation of reason.

The means must always stand under the legislation of the Good, and one can therefore never use evil means for a good purpose, because it is contrary to the order of things. <note>This reflects a classic moral stance: that the "end does not justify the means" if the means themselves are unethical.</note>

Man in the state is an object and his fellow man is a subject: — and interest and self-love must connect the object with the subject; from this follows the rule: Love your neighbor as yourself.

As soon as this order is inverted, I place self-love and interest in the place of the law, make myself the purpose, and use my neighbor as a means. <note>The author argues that using others as tools for one's own gain is the fundamental definition of moral and political disorder.</note>

In this lies the perverted order of things; the foundation of false politics.

True spiritual dignity <note>original: "Geisteswürde"</note> of existence deserves reverence.

# Knowledge of order gives us pure
## concepts of legislation and
## justice.

Who can give wise laws? — No one but he who knows the eternal laws of nature.

True legislation must have the type, number, and weight of human feelings and sensations <note>original: "Empfindungen." In Enlightenment philosophy, this refers to the internal perceptions or feelings that arise from sensory input.</note> as its basis.

If it <note>Referring to legislation or the system of justice.</note> wishes to judge justly, it must know the tension of physical and moral forces toward good and evil, and the degree of resistance that the erring person <note>original: "der Fehlende" — literally the one who is failing or making a mistake.</note> could offer.

How can the phlegmatic <term>phlegmatic: one of the four ancient temperaments, characterized by a calm, cool, or sluggish disposition</term> judge the choleric <term>choleric: a temperament characterized by being quick-tempered, irritable, or highly passionate</term>? How can the old judge the young? The man the woman? How the rich the poor? The person of intellect the fool? — — Everyone judges according to their own feelings and sensations, and everyone judges wrongly. Such laws are like the rabble <note>original: "Pöbel." This term was frequently used by Enlightenment writers to describe the unthinking masses who lack the education or reason to govern themselves.</note>, who are governed only by the noise of great movements and by outward appearances. # I.
## On Forces in General.

To form a correct concept of a <term>force<note>original: "Kräfte". In this metaphysical context, "force" refers to an underlying power, energy, or agency that causes change in the universe, rather than just physical strength.</note></term>, one must abstract from everything material.

We can therefore only imagine a force as an acting being, which we know not in its inner essence, but through its outward manifestation.

All spirits or forces have their origin in the source of all forces.

There are
->divine forces,<-
->spiritual forces,<-
->elemental forces,<-
->physical forces.<-

One force acts indirectly upon another; the divine forces act upon the spiritual; the spiritual upon the elemental forces; the elemental forces upon the physical.

These forces are the <term>principles<note>The fundamental sources or primary elements from which everything else is derived.</note></term> of the four worlds: the divine, the spiritual, the elemental, and the physical world.

All existing objects are nothing more than separated and segregated principles according to time and space, quantity, form, situation, and distance.

These must be divided into giving and receiving, or primitive and secondary forces.

The elementary forces are the expansive, attractive, and repulsive forces.

These three forces, which constitute only a single unity within the power of light, generate the remaining ones: the <term>gyratory<note>original: "gyratoria." Referring to a rotational or whirling motion, often associated in early physics with the movement of celestial bodies or vortices in a fluid ether.</note></term> or vortex force, the explosive or separative force, the formative force, and finally, the resistive force.

These are the seven primal forces of nature; therein lies the mystery of the number 3 within 4, or <note>The text refers to an image of a square containing an equilateral triangle pointing upwards, symbolizing the union of the spiritual trinity (3) and the material quaternary (4) to reach the sacred number seven.</note>

These are the true elementary forces of nature, for through the effect and action of these forces against one another, all compositions, decompositions, and recompositions in nature arise.

These first and primitive forces must necessarily have an organ in the world of appearances through which they act, and a form in which they act.

The organ of the first three primal forces is light; — their form, in which they act in the physical world, is the Sun.

Through this form, physical light and heat are produced. The organ in which light acts is called <term>Mercury<note>original: "Merkurius." In the alchemical tradition, Mercury is not just a planet but a "philosophical" principle representing fluidity, mediation, and the mental or spiritual communication between realms.</note></term>, and the organ in which heat—or life—acts is called <term>Venus<note>original: "Venus." Symbolizing the attractive, cohesive power and the vital warmth necessary for generation and growth.</note></term>. The form in which these two secondary forces are concentrated is the <term>Moon<note>original: "Mond." The Moon was seen as the "sublunary" collector of celestial influences, acting as a container or mirror that reflects higher forces down to Earth.</note></term>.

### 3.
## The Purpose of the Two Primary Forces of Nature.

The two primary forces of nature—namely, the **expansive** and **attractive** forces, through which the entire world is animated and governed—have the same purpose. It consists of union, separation, and reunion; composition, decomposition, and recomposition.

Minerals, vegetables <note>original: "Vegetabilien," referring to the entire plant kingdom</note>, animals, elements, individuals, dead matter, and living force—everything approaches, reunites, and appears under other forms in order to unite once again.

When we observe man, we notice that every individual of his species occupies himself with nothing other than uniting in order to separate again; separating in order to unite again; composing in order to decompose <note>original: "auseinander zu setzen," meaning to take apart or analyze</note>; and decomposing in order to recompose. In this way the spirit occupies itself, and in this way the hands of man occupy themselves with the objects of nature and with man himself. ### 4.
## Physical Forces.

Within nature, a constant movement of both living and inanimate beings prevails. The ebb and flow <note>literally "the inflow and backflow"</note> of the elements, the law of approach and the law of distance—to unite and to separate again—ceaselessly follows the path of immutable laws.

One has as its purpose the composition and formation of things; the other, decomposition and dissolution.

Life and death — movement and rest — composition and dissolution.

And all of this relates to the primary fundamental forces of nature—the expansive and contractive forces. <note>In 18th-century natural philosophy, these forces were often seen as the "breath" of the universe, alternating between pulling inward and pushing outward.</note>

Through the contractive force, or the minus, nature attracts, brings components closer together, and gathers matter.

Through the expansive force, she divides, repels, decomposes what is compounded, and, through homogeneity, brings the simple back to the simple.

**The Law of Unity shows us the entire essence of the miraculous, and unveils all the secrets of magic.**

# Organology of Nature,

### or

### I.
### Sketch of the Organology of Nature.

**W**e can have correct concepts neither of God nor of Nature if we do not know the eternal order of the primal origin of all things.

This we learn, however, through the laws of unity and its manifestation of power, which is Nature.

In everything that exists within Nature, we notice:
1. A force that acts.
2. An <term>organ<note>original: "Organ"; in this context, it refers to the instrument or medium through which a natural force expresses itself.</note></term> through which it acts.
3. A form in which it acts.
4. A purpose for which it acts.
5. A relationship according to which it acts.
6. An order that it effects—
7. in the internal, or spiritual realm,
8. in the external, or physical realm, whereby
9. the properties
10. of every existing thing are determined.

This is the primary outline of Creation, because it lies at the foundation of all things.

<summary>This page introduces the concept of "Organology," asserting that understanding the divine and natural worlds requires grasping the laws of unity and force. It provides a ten-point structural outline of how forces manifest through organs and forms to create the order of the universe.</summary>
<keywords>organology, nature, creation, unity, spiritual vs physical, manifestation of force, teleology, natural philosophy</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the numbered exploration of "Organology" introduced on the previous page, detailing how the manifestation of force progresses through stages of time, space, and order.</meta>

1. Force becomes the cause of existence.
2. The organ — the cause of actual being <note>original: "Daseyn"; in German philosophy, this often refers to "being here" or a specific, concrete presence in the world as opposed to abstract existence.</note>.
3. Form, the law of existence.
4. Purpose, the cause of realization.
5. Relationship, the ground of equality <note>or parity; the underlying principle that allows different things to be compared or balanced.</note>.
6. Order — the ground of harmony, proportion, regularity; through which everything that exists
7. in the internal, or spiritual,
8. in the external, or material,
9. through its properties
10. reveals itself as an existing thing.

Without this progression nothing can exist; it is the law of stages <term>Stuffengesetz<note>A concept suggesting that nature and spirit develop through a hierarchy of specific steps or evolutionary levels.</note></term> of the manifestation of force.

This fundamental law manifests through just as many stages, such as:

1. Outside of time and space.
2. In time.
3. In space.
4. In time and space.
5. In space and time.
6. In order, harmony, regularity, proportion.
7. In the internal or spiritual.
8. In the external or material.

### The Plus and Minus in Nature.

"Plus" is the name given to that force which always grows as long as the energy of the central force <note>The "central force" likely refers to the source of expansion or the point of origin for the "plus" energy.</note> lasts. At the point where that energy ceases is the maximum of the force; and this plus-force in nature is the expansive force.

Where the energy ceases, the "Minus"—or the attractive force—begins: the counter-action, which relates to the energy of the first force, and which hastens from the periphery to the center, always decreasing, and is therefore called "Minus."

<keywords>primordial force, divine realm, spiritual realm, elemental realm, physical realm, expansive force, attractive force, plus and minus, polarity, central force</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the "Plus" (expansive) and "Minus" (attractive) forces introduced on the previous page, specifically detailing how light acts as the central source that generates these dynamics to create motion and life.</meta>

These two primary forces <term>Hauptkräfte: The core, governing powers of the physical world.</term> are the components of motion. They constitute action and reaction in nature.

Light is the central force of the first motion, and consequently generates the two forces that constitute motion.

The point where the energy of the expansive force ceases is called the maximum of the expansive force:

the point where the action from the periphery to the center, or the reaction, ceases, is the maximum of the attractive force.

From expansion, attraction, and repulsion arises, as we have explained, all life in nature.

The first fundamental forces of nature are therefore established as follows —

1. Light.
2. Expansive and attractive force.

Since there exists in *nature* a *gradation* <term>Gradation: A gradual progression or scale of intensity between two poles.</term> from the *expansive force* to its *maximum*, and from the *attractive force* back to its *maximum*, we perceive — —

that between the *expansive force* up to its *maximum* — from the *maximum* to *attraction*, and from *attraction* up to the *maximum* of the *attractive force*, there must be *intermediate forces* <term>Intermediate forces: Called "Mittelkräfte" in the original; these are the transitional energies that bridge the gap between pure expansion and pure attraction.</term>.

These 3 *intermediate forces*, combined with the *primary forces*, constitute the 7 *primordial forces* <term>Primordial forces: "Urkräfte," the original, fundamental powers that underpin all of creation.</term> of *nature*.

The *expansive force* and its *maximum* constitute the *action* in *nature*:

The *attractive force* <note>original: "Attraktionskraft"</note> and its *maximum* constitute the *reaction*.

Since everything in *nature* consists of *action* and *reaction*, the *forces* in their *operation* relate to one another in the following manner:

<gloss>1</gloss> *Expansive Force*, <gloss>2</gloss> *Attraction*, <gloss>3</gloss> *Repulsion*, <gloss>4</gloss> *Circular motion* <note>original: "Zirkelbewegung"</note>,
<gloss>5</gloss> *Explosion*, <gloss>6</gloss> *Formation* <note>original: "Formirung"</note>, <gloss>7</gloss> *Substantial force*.

The first 3 *forces* — namely: *expansion*, *attraction*, and *repulsion* — are the *animating*, or *inner*, *spiritual forces*.

*Circular motion*, *explosion*, and *formation* — are the *shaping*, or *material forces*.

The first are *active*; the second *passive*.

Therein consists that which is called *male* and *female* in *nature*.

## I.
## On the Method of Invention in General.

Invention can be viewed as both a <term>science<note>original: "Wissenschaft"</note></term> and an <term>art<note>original: "Kunst"</note></term>.

As a science, it is the sum total of those rules by which one can derive new truths from known ones:

As an art, it is the skill of practicing these rules, or of deriving new truths from known ones.

The invention of new truths presupposes truths already known.

The entire <term>art of invention<note>The author uses "Erfindungskunst" to describe heuristics—the systematic method of discovery and problem-solving.</note></term> consists of bringing a known premise into a known equation with the laws of nature; from this, we find a progression of unknowns, which we must then reduce to the object being sought. These reductions are again identified with the laws of nature, and we obtain the truth, as the examples demonstrate. However, everything must first be divided into classes.

When we seek a truth, we are seeking either <term>concepts<note>original: "Begriffe"</note></term> or <term>propositions<note>original: "Sätze"</note></term>:

<sig>P 2</sig>
<meta>catchword: Fe-</meta>

<summary>This page defines the "art of invention" (heuristics) as both a theoretical science of rules and a practical skill for deriving new information from existing truths. It outlines a process of using natural laws and equations to move from known premises to new discoveries.</summary>

<keywords>heuristics, art of invention, methodology, logic, laws of nature, scientific discovery, concepts, propositions</keywords>

4. The intention toward which one seeks to direct it.

In regard to searching, one observes the following rules. One has:

1. An intention—one seeks the requirements of the means.
2. An effect—the requirements of the causes, machines, and instruments.
3. Properties—the requirements of the principles.
4. A predicate—the requirements of the subject.
5. The task—the requirements of the method and the sources of the resolution <note>original: "Auflösung," referring here to the solution of a problem or the completion of a logical task</note>.

When I wish to invent <note>In this context, "erfinden" refers to both mechanical invention and the logical discovery of new truths</note> something, I have three objects: that which is sought, the known, and the unknown.

These three objects relate to one another in nature as: <gloss>1</gloss> law, <gloss>2</gloss> means, <gloss>3</gloss> purpose.

The <gloss>1</gloss> unknown, the <gloss>2</gloss> known, the <gloss>3</gloss> sought-after.

Now, if I identify the known with the unknown, I obtain that which is sought.

If I add the means to the law, the result is the purpose.

Thus, the first rule is: I must seek to identify the known with the unknown.

### 2.

## On the Discovery of Truth.

There is no thing in nature that does not already contain within itself all the questions and answers that one can ask about it—either affirmative or negative. "This I am; this I am not."

The constituent parts <note>original: "Bestandtheile"</note> constitute the exterior of things.

The properties constitute the interior. The construction of nature behaves according to the same laws in both cases.

Therefore, if I bring my question about an object into an <term>equation<note>original: "Aequation." In this context, the author refers to a logical balancing or alignment between the mind's inquiry and the structure of the physical world.</note></term> with the constructions of nature, the result of combining my question with nature's construction must provide the specific answer regarding the sought-after constituent parts or properties.

The matter proceeds as naturally as in arithmetic.

I ask: how much is 2 times 2?

->2 times 2<-
---
->4<-

2 is the arithmetic progression; my question is: what is 2 and 2? Thus, I apply my question to the progression, and the result is 4—the correct answer.

<note>The author uses a simple mathematical analogy to argue that "truth" is not created, but rather "solved" like a math problem by aligning human logic with the existing laws of nature.</note>

### 3.

## On the Solution of Problems.

If the building of concepts could be arranged like the building of numbers, said the famous mathematician <note>Johann Heinrich Lambert (1728–1777) was a Swiss polymath who sought to apply mathematical rigor to philosophy and logic.</note> Lambert, then one would find a paved path in the discovery of infinitely many truths.

Number theory shows us the way to arrange all concepts through equations according to numerical laws. Through it, we can therefore think of everything possible.

In the construction of every thing in nature, there already lie all possible questions and answers about an object—about which the question is asked, and to which an answer shall be given.

I can raise no question about an object that does not relate to the essence, property, or relationship of the thing—that does not concern the interior or exterior of the same, such as: Cause, effect, consequence, purpose, relationship, order <term>etc.<note>The original uses "2c.", a common historical shorthand for "et cetera."</note></term> or: Force, organ, form, realization, difference, proportion.

Therefore, if the question regarding the order of nature's constructions is identified through comparisons, then the numbers—acting as representative images of the things about which questions are asked and answers are to be given—necessarily provide the solution to the problems.

### 4.
## To what extent the Calculus of Nature is a science.

Just as numerical calculation <note>original: "Zahlenrechnung," referring to basic arithmetic or the manipulation of numbers.</note> is called a science by many—one which teaches the comparisons of numbers and the changes arising from them—so too can we call the Calculus of Nature <note>Calculus here refers to a systematic method of reasoning or computation applied to the laws of the natural world rather than modern infinitesimal calculus.</note> a science. This science teaches how one should hold concepts against one another according to the constructions of nature, compare them with one another, identify them with the same, and derive their properties from them.

### 5.
## The theory of numbers viewed systematically.

Every science and every part thereof can be viewed as a system, insofar as a system is the sum total <note>original: "Innbegriff," the essential collection or embodiment of ideas.</note> of ideas and propositions that, taken together, can be viewed as a whole.

In a system, there must be subordination <note>The hierarchical ranking of specific ideas under general ones.</note> and connection. It is "simple" if one treats a single matter without further subdivision; it is "composite" if one examines it through its branches.

The fundamental rule of the system consists in this: that what precedes shall make clear what follows in regard to the understanding—

->certain in regard to reason—<-
->possible in regard to practice.<- <note>The author distinguishes between three levels of validity: logical clarity for the *Understanding* (Verstand), philosophical certainty for the higher faculty of *Reason* (Vernunft), and feasibility in *Practice* or application.</note>

### How man must observe the objects of nature in order to find truth.

One observes that in nature, everything moves from the simple to the manifold, and returns again from the manifold to the simple.

According to the very same law by which nature produces everything progressively, man must observe things if he wishes to find truth.

The ancients <note>A reference to classical philosophers, likely reflecting the Scholastic definition of truth as "adaequatio rei et intellectus" (the correspondence of the thing and the mind).</note> said that truth consists in the agreement of that which follows with that which precedes.

When my words agree with my heart, and my heart agrees with my opinion <note>original: "Meynung," an archaic spelling of *Meinung* (opinion or conviction).</note>, then they are true.

### 7.

## On the Possible in Nature.

Everything possible is already present in nature according to unchangeable laws.

That which exists only exists because it is possible.

Therefore, the possible and the existing have the same laws; only the possible lies at the foundation of the existing—that is to say: every thing exists according to the laws of possibility.

Possibility is therefore the cause—existence the consequence—the effect is the bond that links cause and consequence together——or possibility and reality.

In this way, the present connects the past and the future. — Present, past, and future

## On Analysis in the Theory of Numbers.

All our knowledge begins with the senses and ascends from individual concepts through various paths to the universal. These paths, taken together, belong to the analytical method.

The properties that we notice in natural things are grounded both in one another and in the nature of things.

This nature is itself grounded in the composition of the parts within the body, and the various kinds of natural effects are grounded in general laws. These laws must then have a basis from which they become necessary.

This basis is the unity of nature, which expresses itself in all its effects according to always identical proportions; and just as we have thus far obtained an ascending analysis through experience, by which we discovered the possible within the real, so we also obtain a descending analysis, which teaches us through the <term>chained relationships<note>original: "Kettenverhältnisse," referring to the interconnected series of cause and effect that link all phenomena in a "chain of being."</note></term> of all things how the possible becomes real.

The first is the analysis of experience; that of the <term>theory of numbers<note>original: "Zahlenlehre." In this context, it refers not just to simple arithmetic, but to the rational, mathematical structure of the universe as understood through pure reason.</note></term> is the analysis of reason. Through the first, we ascend from the real to the possible; through the second, we descend from the possible to the real.

### 9.

## Explanations and Additions to the Analysis of Nature.

The logical analytics of the <term>calculus of ideas<note>original: "Calcul der Ideen." This refers to a formal system of logic, influenced by thinkers like Leibniz, where reasoning is treated as a form of mathematical calculation to ensure certainty.</note></term>, or the theory of numbers, is an art of deriving unknown or sought-after concepts from those that are already known or given.

### First Addition.

Because nothing is invented out of nothing, certain concepts must be provided as a foundation in order to discover those that are currently unknown.

### Second Addition.

Since unknown concepts must be derived from known ones, it is clear that they must possess a certain <term>relation<note>original: "Relation." In this context, it refers to a necessary logical link or mathematical ratio between two ideas.</note></term> or connection with them; and

### Third Addition

because logical analytics is performed by means of <term>identities<note>original: "Identitäten." This refers to the logical principle where a complex concept is shown to be identical to a set of simpler, known components (A = B + C).</note></term>, these relations must be of such a nature that the known and unknown concepts can be identified with one another through them.

We have explained that <term>relation<note>original: "Relatio."</note></term> is a composite ratio. Therefore, the relations in this logical calculus form the numbers, which consist of the composition of simple <term>fundamental forces<note>original: "Grundkräfte." The author posits that the physical and intellectual world is built from basic forces that combine in precise, numerical proportions.</note></term>.

### Explanation.

General analytics is the art of deriving other concepts from those that are universal and indefinite.

## 10.
## On Relations, and How They Are Considered in the Theory of Numbers.

Everything in nature becomes recognizable to us through **relations**, and these relations are equivalent to **numerical progression**.
->1, 2, 3, 4, 5.<-

As the relations are, so are the **proportions**; for proportions are merely the identities of relations.

The same laws are found everywhere.

A **simple** relation is one that includes only a single concept within itself.

A **simply composite** relation is one that consists of several connected concepts.

### II.

## On the Relations in the Calculus of Nature,
## Compared with Arithmetical and Geometrical
## Relations.

When one investigates through subtraction how much one number is greater than another, one views these two numbers in their **arithmetical relation**:

But when one investigates through division how often one number is contained within another, or what part of one number resides in the other, one views them in their **geometrical relation**.

If, however, one simply observes a **progression** <note>A series or sequence of steps.</note> in its increased state compared to the previous one, then this observation is the consideration of a conceivable relation.

From these relations arise all possible **concepts**, which are merely comparisons of things according to the order of progression in nature.

->All concepts are limited<-
->to the understanding,<- <note>In Enlightenment philosophy, the "understanding" (Verstand) is the faculty of the mind that organizes sensory data into concepts.</note>

### 12.
### Of Magnitudes.

Whatever is capable of increase or decrease, mathematics calls a magnitude <note>German: *Größe*. This term refers to any quantity that can be measured or compared.</note>. This distinguishes things in which one otherwise perceives nothing distinct—for example, one quantity of ducats <note>Gold coins used as currency throughout Europe from the Middle Ages until the 20th century.</note> from another quantity of ducats, all of which have the same stamp and weight.

All magnitudes are based on numbers, for numbers constitute magnitudes; and all numbers are based on a unit <note>German: *Einheit*. In Enlightenment philosophy, the "unit" or "one" was often seen as the indivisible starting point of all complexity.</note>, which has no magnitude itself but can only be considered as a force, which in its manifestation forms the magnitudes.

How large a thing is, we discover either through the immediate representation that we have of the thing itself, or through comparison with another known magnitude.

In nature there are
